title: Guru Har Krishan's gurpurab
hook: remembered with care for the sick at Bangla Sahib

segments.voice: Yesterday, Har Rai, and your line: the healer. Did you care for one living thing without asking whose side it was on? Today, his son, the youngest of all the Gurus. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

In the middle of New Delhi, there's a white gurdwara with a golden dome and a large pool. Day and night, people come with bottles to take its water home to someone sick. Its langar hall serves meals from morning to night. And the whole place is built around the memory of a child, who came to Delhi because an emperor summoned him, and stayed to look after the sick. Today: Guru Har Krishan's gurpurab.
screen: `A WHITE GURDWARA IN NEW DELHI.` → `BOTTLES OF WATER FOR THE SICK.` → `THE MEMORY OF A CHILD.`

segments.voice: Guru Har Krishan was the younger son of Guru Har Rai. Before his father died, he named the boy as the eighth Guru; tradition says he was about five. Some objected, including his older brother, Ram Rai, who had gone to the Mughal court and won favor there. The emperor Aurangzeb summoned the young Guru to Delhi. In Delhi, he stayed at the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh, a Rajput noble. That house is now Gurdwara Bangla Sahib: bangla means bungalow. While he was there, an epidemic struck the city; tradition usually names smallpox, and some accounts say cholera. Tradition says the child Guru went out among the sick, of every faith, giving water and comfort and care. He caught the disease himself and died, still a child; tradition says he was about eight. Tradition says his last words, when asked who would follow him, were Baba Bakale: the next Guru is at Bakala, which proved to be Guru Tegh Bahadur. The Sikh Ardas, which you learned line by line this year, remembers him in a single line. In paraphrase: remember Guru Har Krishan, at the sight of whom all suffering departs. Today, the pool at Bangla Sahib is where people take water for the sick, in his memory. His gurpurab is marked there with kirtan and with the langar, and some Sikhs visit or serve the sick that day. A very short life, remembered for care that walked toward the sickness instead of away from it.
screen: `THE EIGHTH GURU, AT FIVE.` · `A BUNGALOW IN DELHI.` · `AMONG THE SICK, AND STRICKEN.` · `REMEMBERED IN THE ARDAS.` · then, large: `THE CHILD HEALER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone unwell. Sit, and bring to mind one person you know who's sick, recovering or worn out. Picture them clearly. Then think of one small, real thing that would help: a message, a meal, a ride, an errand, an hour of company. Decide when you'll do it. Hold them in your mind with care until the bell. If you pray, you can say the Ardas line for them in your own way, or just Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Guru Har Krishan's gurpurab. The eighth Guru's birthday, remembered at Bangla Sahib in Delhi, where the child Guru cared for the sick in an epidemic.
Your line: the child healer. Today, do the one small thing you chose for someone who's unwell. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: On Guru Har Krishan's gurpurab, Sikhs gather at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi and elsewhere for kirtan and langar; many take water from Bangla Sahib's pool to the sick and serve the unwell in his memory.

what a scholar hears: sources differ on smallpox or cholera; the Ardas line on Guru Har Krishan comes from Var Sri Bhagauti Ji, which Sikhs attribute to the Tenth Guru.
